```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")
```

A regression line is only the start. Before believing it you want to know if
the line fits the middle and the edges equally well, if the residuals have the
shape the model assumes, and if something the model ignores is still sitting in
them. Each of those questions has its standard plot, and they read best side by
side, as one figure about one model.

The model is a classic: diamond price against weight on log–log axes, fitted to
the 53,940 stones of `ggplot2::diamonds`.

```{r}
dm <- as.data.frame(ggplot2::diamonds)
dm$lcarat <- log10(dm$carat)
dm$lprice <- log10(dm$price)

fit <- lm(lprice ~ lcarat, data = dm)
dm$fitted <- fitted(fit)
dm$resid <- resid(fit)

coef(fit)
summary(fit)$r.squared
```

A slope of 1.68: a stone twice as heavy costs about 2^1.68^ ≈ 3.2 times as
much. The
fit explains 93% of the variance in log price. Now the four checks.

## What is drawn

- **A, the data and the fit.** With 54,000 points a scatter is one blob, so
  `mark_density_2d_filled()` draws the 2-D kernel density as filled bands
  instead. `contour_var = "ndensity"` scales the density to 0–1 and the
  `breaks` start at 0.02, so the near-empty background is left unfilled.
  `mark_quantile()` adds quantile regression lines for the 10th, 50th and 90th
  percentiles (`quantreg::rq()`). If those lines run parallel, the spread
  around the fit is the same for small and large stones.
- **B, residuals against fitted values**, with the same density bands and
  quantile lines. A good fit shows a flat band centred on zero.
- **C, a normal Q–Q plot of the residuals.** `mark_qq()` plots sample
  quantiles against normal quantiles and `mark_qq_line()` draws the line
  through the quartiles. Points on the line mean normal residuals.
- **D, residual ECDFs by cut.** `mark_ecdf()` draws one empirical cumulative
  distribution per colour. If cut did not matter once weight is known, the five
  curves would lie on top of each other.

```{r}
ramp <- c("#f4ecd8", "#e3cfa4", "#c9a874", "#a07a46", "#6b4f2c", "#3b2a1a")
bands <- c(0.02, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)

a <- vplot(dm, width = 4, height = 3.4) |>
  mark_density_2d_filled(x = lcarat, y = lprice,
                         contour_var = "ndensity", breaks = bands) |>
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = ramp) |>
  mark_quantile(x = lcarat, y = lprice, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9),
                color = "#8c2d19", linewidth = 0.6) |>
  labs(x = "log10 carat", y = "log10 price (USD)") |>
  theme_minimal() |>
  theme(legend.position = "none")

b <- vplot(dm, width = 4, height = 3.4) |>
  mark_density_2d_filled(x = fitted, y = resid,
                         contour_var = "ndensity", breaks = bands) |>
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = ramp) |>
  mark_quantile(x = fitted, y = resid, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9),
                color = "#8c2d19", linewidth = 0.6) |>
  labs(x = "fitted log10 price", y = "residual") |>
  theme_minimal() |>
  theme(legend.position = "none")

c <- vplot(dm, width = 4, height = 3.4) |>
  mark_qq(sample = resid, color = "#a07a46", size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) |>
  mark_qq_line(sample = resid, color = "#8c2d19") |>
  labs(x = "normal quantile", y = "residual quantile") |>
  theme_minimal()

d <- vplot(dm, width = 4, height = 3.4) |>
  mark_ecdf(x = resid, color = cut) |>
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#d9c7a2", "#c9a874", "#a07a46", "#6b4f2c", "#3b2a1a")) |>
  labs(x = "residual", y = "share of diamonds", color = "cut") |>
  theme_minimal()

diagnostics <- concat(a, b, c, d, ncol = 2, guides = "keep") |>
  compose_annotation(
    title = "Diagnosing a power law for diamond prices",
    subtitle = "lm(log10(price) ~ log10(carat)) on 53,940 diamonds",
    tag_levels = "A"
  )
```

`concat()` lines the four panels up on a shared grid, so the axes of A and C, and
of B and D, sit on the same vertical. `compose_annotation()` puts one title over
all of them and letters the panels for the text to refer to.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Four-panel diagnostic figure. A: filled density of log price against log carat with three nearly parallel quantile lines. B: residuals against fitted values, a flat band around zero. C: normal Q-Q plot of residuals bending away from the line in both tails. D: five residual ECDF curves by cut, Fair shifted left and Ideal right."
vg(diagnostics, "model-diagnostics", dpi = 130)
```

## Reading it

**A and B: the line fits, and the spread is even.** The 10th, 50th and 90th
percentile lines have slopes of 1.69, 1.65 and 1.72, close to parallel. The band
between them is about 0.29 on the log10 scale, a factor of two in price, for a
0.3-carat stone and a 2-carat one alike. In B the band is flat and centred on
zero. The clumps along both panels are real: diamonds are cut to popular
weights, so the data piles up at 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1 and 1.5 carats.

**C: the tails are heavier than normal.** The middle 95% of the residuals sit
on the line. Beyond about two standard deviations they bend away on both sides:
there are more very cheap and very expensive stones for their weight than a
normal distribution allows. Standard errors from `summary(fit)` assume normal
residuals, so they will be a little optimistic here; the coefficients themselves
are fine.

**D: cut is still in the residuals.** The five curves are shifted, in order.
The median residual of a Fair stone is −0.10 on the log10 scale and that of an
Ideal stone +0.02. At the same weight, an Ideal cut costs about a third more than
a Fair one. That is a variable the model should include. The next model would add
`cut` (and colour and clarity, which do the same thing), and the four panels would
be drawn again.

For each mark on its own, see [density curve](density.qmd),
[contours](contours.qmd) and [marginal distributions](marginal.qmd).
